blocks.text: A 29-year-old with a gastrin-secreting tumour has recurrent duodenal ulcers and watery diarrhoea, because her stomach is producing acid far beyond what the meal demands and the excess destroys pancreatic enzymes in the small bowel. Digestive juices are powerful, so the body controls their cells, their timing and their switch-off signals with great precision.

blocks.markdown: **Saliva.** Three pairs of major glands (parotid, submandibular, sublingual) secrete about 1-1.5 L/day. Acinar cells secrete an isotonic fluid, and the ducts then reabsorb Na+ and Cl- and secrete K+ and HCO3-, so the final saliva is **hypotonic** with a slightly alkaline pH. Its contents include **salivary amylase** (starts starch digestion), **lingual lipase**, **mucins** (lubrication), **lysozyme, lactoferrin and IgA** (defence) and bicarbonate (buffering of oesophageal acid). Saliva is controlled by the autonomic nervous system: **parasympathetic stimulation** gives a copious watery secretion, while sympathetic stimulation gives a smaller, more viscous secretion; unusually, both stimulate secretion.

blocks.title: Cells of the gastric gland
blocks.text: Parietal (oxyntic) cells secrete hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor. Chief (peptic) cells secrete pepsinogen and gastric lipase. Mucous neck cells and surface cells secrete mucus and bicarbonate. Enteroendocrine cells include G cells (gastrin, mainly antrum), enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cells (histamine) and D cells (somatostatin).

blocks.markdown: **Making acid.** In the parietal cell, carbonic anhydrase combines CO2 and water to make H+ and HCO3-. The H+ is pumped into the lumen by the apical **H+/K+ ATPase (proton pump)**, while HCO3- leaves across the basolateral membrane in exchange for Cl-, which then reaches the lumen. For each H+ secreted, one HCO3- enters the blood (the **alkaline tide**), so repeated vomiting of gastric acid causes metabolic alkalosis. Three signals stimulate the parietal cell: **acetylcholine** (vagus, M3 receptors), **gastrin** (from G cells) and **histamine** (from ECL cells, H2 receptors). Histamine-blocking and proton-pump drugs (pharmacology teaching examples) reduce acid by acting on the last two steps. Acid converts **pepsinogen** to active **pepsin** (optimum pH about 2) and kills ingested organisms; intrinsic factor is needed for vitamin B12 absorption.

blocks.caption: pH from the hydrogen ion concentration in mol/L. A change of one pH unit is a tenfold change in [H+].

blocks.title: pH of gastric juice
blocks.prompt: A sample of gastric juice has [H+] = 0.07 mol/L. Calculate its pH, and say how much more concentrated in H+ it is than blood at pH 7.4.

steps.text: Find the pH difference from blood.

A difference of 6.25 pH units is a factor of 10^6.25, roughly 1.8 million, so H+ concentration in gastric juice is on the order of a million times that of blood, which is why parietal cells need an ATP-driven pump.

blocks.answer: pH is about 1.15, and gastric juice has roughly 10^6 times the H+ concentration of blood.

blocks.markdown:
**Regulation: the three phases of gastric acid secretion.**

- **Cephalic phase** (about 30%): sight, smell, taste and thought activate the vagus; acetylcholine stimulates parietal cells directly, ECL cells, and G cells through gastrin-releasing peptide.
- **Gastric phase** (about 60%): distension and the presence of peptides and amino acids stimulate G cells and local and vagal reflexes. Gastrin raises acid secretion. Antral pH below about 2 stimulates D cells to release somatostatin, which inhibits gastrin and acid (negative feedback).
- **Intestinal phase** (about 10%): initially stimulatory (amino acids), but mainly **inhibitory**: acid, fat and hypertonic chyme in the duodenum release **secretin**, **CCK** and GIP and trigger neural reflexes that slow gastric emptying and reduce acid.

The percentages are approximate.

blocks.caption: The three digestive hormones.
rows: Peptides and amino acids, distension, vagus (GRP); inhibited by pH below about 2
Stimulates parietal cell acid (directly and via ECL histamine); trophic to gastric mucosa
Stimulates pancreatic duct and bile duct bicarbonate secretion; inhibits gastric acid; neutralises chyme
Fatty acids and amino acids in the duodenum
Stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion and gallbladder contraction; relaxes the sphincter of Oddi; slows gastric emptying

blocks.markdown: **Pancreatic secretion.** The exocrine pancreas has two components. **Acinar cells** secrete enzymes in a small volume: trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen, procarboxypeptidases (protein), **amylase** (starch), **lipase** with colipase and phospholipase A2 (fat), and nucleases. Proteases are secreted as inactive proenzymes so they do not digest the pancreas itself; **enteropeptidase** on the duodenal brush border converts trypsinogen to **trypsin**, which activates the other proenzymes. **Duct cells** secrete a watery, bicarbonate-rich fluid (about 1-1.5 L/day in total) that neutralises gastric acid so pancreatic enzymes, which prefer a near-neutral pH, can work. Secretin drives the bicarbonate component, and CCK (with vagal acetylcholine) drives the enzyme component.

blocks.title: Predicting responses to acid and fat in the duodenum
blocks.prompt: Acidic chyme containing fat enters the duodenum. Predict which hormones are released and the effects on the pancreas, gallbladder and stomach.

steps.text: Duodenal acid stimulates S cells to release secretin, which acts on pancreatic and biliary ducts to produce bicarbonate-rich fluid, neutralising the acid.
Fatty acids stimulate I cells to release CCK, which causes gallbladder contraction, relaxation of the sphincter of Oddi, and acinar secretion of enzymes including lipase.
Both hormones also inhibit gastric acid secretion and slow gastric emptying, so the duodenum is not overloaded (the intestinal phase of inhibition).

blocks.answer: Secretin (bicarbonate) and CCK (enzymes, bile release) are released; gastric acid secretion and emptying are reduced.

items: Saliva: hypotonic, amylase, lingual lipase, mucin, lysozyme, IgA; stimulated by both divisions of the autonomic nervous system.
Parietal cells: HCl (H+/K+ ATPase) and intrinsic factor; stimulated by ACh, gastrin and histamine.
Chief cells: pepsinogen and gastric lipase; mucous cells: mucus and bicarbonate protective layer.
Pancreas: enzyme-rich acinar fluid (CCK) and bicarbonate-rich duct fluid (secretin).
Cephalic, gastric and intestinal phases regulate acid, with the intestinal phase mainly inhibitory.

blocks.title: Control is built on feedback
blocks.text: Acid is the key signal in both directions: it is stimulated by gastrin, but low antral pH inhibits gastrin through somatostatin, and acid in the duodenum releases secretin and CCK, which inhibit the stomach. This is why drugs that suppress acid can raise gastrin levels.

blocks.title: Enzymes versus bicarbonate
blocks.text: Secretin and CCK have different targets: secretin mainly increases bicarbonate and fluid from duct cells, whereas CCK mainly increases enzyme secretion from acinar cells and gallbladder contraction. Do not state that the same hormone does both.

points: Saliva is a hypotonic, amylase- and mucin-containing fluid controlled by both parasympathetic and sympathetic nerves.
Parietal cells make HCl and intrinsic factor, chief cells make pepsinogen, G cells make gastrin and ECL cells make histamine; each H+ secreted gives one HCO3- to the blood.
Gastric acid is controlled in cephalic, gastric and intestinal phases, with negative feedback from low pH, somatostatin, secretin and CCK.
Gastrin stimulates acid, secretin stimulates pancreatic bicarbonate, and CCK stimulates pancreatic enzymes and gallbladder contraction.

questions.stem: Which cell of the gastric gland secretes both hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: parietal cells secrete both acid and intrinsic factor.
distractorRationale.b: Chief cells secrete pepsinogen and gastric lipase.

questions.explanation: Parietal (oxyntic) cells make HCl through the H+/K+ ATPase and also secrete intrinsic factor, which is required for vitamin B12 absorption in the terminal ileum. Chief cells make pepsinogen, which acid converts to pepsin.

questions.stem: A man eats a large steak. Which event is the principal trigger of the gastric phase of acid secretion?

options.text: Gastric distension and peptides stimulating G cells and vagal reflexes
The smell and sight of food acting via the vagus
Fat in the duodenum releasing CCK

questions.correctOptionText: Gastric distension and peptides stimulating G cells and vagal reflexes

distractorRationale.a: Correct: this accounts for the largest share of meal-stimulated acid.
distractorRationale.c: CCK is an intestinal-phase signal that inhibits gastric emptying and acid.
distractorRationale.d: Secretin from duodenal acid inhibits gastric acid, part of the intestinal phase.

questions.explanation: In the gastric phase, stretch and peptide/amino acid products of protein digestion stimulate gastrin release and vagal reflexes, and gastrin acts on parietal cells directly and via ECL histamine. The cephalic and intestinal phases account for smaller proportions.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman eats a very fatty meal. Which hormone response best explains subsequent gallbladder contraction and release of lipase-rich pancreatic fluid?

options.text: Release of CCK from duodenal I cells in response to fatty acids
Release of gastrin from antral G cells in response to fat
Release of secretin from S cells in response to fat
Release of somatostatin from D cells in response to fat

questions.correctOptionText: Release of CCK from duodenal I cells in response to fatty acids

distractorRationale.a: Correct: CCK contracts the gallbladder, relaxes the sphincter of Oddi and stimulates acinar enzyme secretion.
distractorRationale.b: Gastrin is released by peptides and distension and acts on acid secretion.
distractorRationale.c: Secretin responds to acid and mainly increases bicarbonate.
distractorRationale.d: Somatostatin is inhibitory and is not the trigger for gallbladder contraction.

questions.explanation: Fatty acids and amino acids in the duodenum stimulate I cells to release cholecystokinin. CCK causes gallbladder contraction, relaxation of the sphincter of Oddi and enzyme secretion from pancreatic acinar cells, which together support fat digestion.

questions.stem: Which factor describes how trypsinogen is activated within the duodenal lumen?

options.text: Enteropeptidase on the brush border converts it to trypsin, which then activates other proenzymes
Pepsin in the duodenum converts it to trypsin
Secretin directly cleaves it to trypsin
Gastrin binds it and activates it

questions.correctOptionText: Enteropeptidase on the brush border converts it to trypsin, which then activates other proenzymes

distractorRationale.a: Correct: this keeps proteases inactive until they reach the duodenum.
distractorRationale.b: Pepsin is inactivated at the duodenal pH and is not the activator.
distractorRationale.c: Secretin is a hormone that regulates secretion; it is not an enzyme.
distractorRationale.d: Gastrin is a peptide hormone and does not activate enzymes.

questions.explanation: Pancreatic proteases are stored and secreted as inactive proenzymes to protect the gland. Enteropeptidase, a brush border enzyme in the duodenum, activates trypsinogen to trypsin, and trypsin then activates chymotrypsinogen and the other proenzymes.

questions.stem: A fall in antral pH below about 2 inhibits gastrin release, providing negative feedback on acid secretion.
questions.explanation: Low antral pH stimulates D cells to release somatostatin, which inhibits G cells and so reduces gastrin and acid secretion. When acid is suppressed with drugs, this brake is lost and gastrin levels rise.

questions.stem: A drug raises the gastric pH from 1.0 to 4.0. By what factor does the hydrogen ion concentration in the gastric lumen fall?
questions.explanation: pH is the negative logarithm of [H+], so a rise of 3 pH units corresponds to a factor of 10^3 = 1000 fall in [H+]. This large change explains why acid suppression has such a marked effect on pepsin activity, which depends on low pH.

questions.stem: Assume a person secretes 1.5 L of gastric juice per day containing 100 mmol/L of H+. For each H+ secreted by parietal cells, one HCO3- enters the blood. How many mmol of HCO3- enter the blood from this secretion per day?
questions.explanation: H+ secreted is 1.5 L x 100 mmol/L = 150 mmol/day, and each H+ secreted generates one HCO3- (via carbonic anhydrase) that leaves the basolateral membrane, so 150 mmol/day enter the blood. This alkaline tide is normally neutralised when the acid is later reabsorbed or when pancreatic bicarbonate is secreted, but persistent vomiting of gastric acid leads to metabolic alkalosis.

questions.stem: Name the cell types of a gastric gland and give the secretory product and one function of each, and name the three stimulants of the parietal cell.
markingGuide: Parietal cell: HCl and intrinsic factor (acid kills microbes, activates pepsin; intrinsic factor for B12 absorption)
Chief cell: pepsinogen (and gastric lipase); pepsinogen is activated by acid to pepsin, which digests protein
Mucous neck/surface cells: mucus and bicarbonate, protecting the mucosa
G cells: gastrin; ECL cells: histamine; D cells: somatostatin
Parietal cell stimulants: acetylcholine, gastrin and histamine
questions.explanation: The gland combines exocrine cells that make the juice with endocrine and paracrine cells that tune it. Knowing the product of each cell allows prediction of the effects of loss of that cell type.

questions.stem: Describe the cephalic, gastric and intestinal phases of gastric acid secretion, including the neural and hormonal mediators of each and how the process is switched off.
markingGuide: Cephalic phase (about 30%): sight, smell, taste and thought; vagus releases ACh onto parietal cells, ECL cells and G cells (via gastrin-releasing peptide)
Gastric phase (about 60%): distension and peptides/amino acids stimulate gastrin release and local/vagal reflexes
Gastrin stimulates parietal cells directly and through ECL histamine
Intestinal phase (about 10%): initially stimulatory, then inhibitory via secretin, CCK, GIP and neural reflexes when acid, fat or hypertonic chyme enter the duodenum
Switch-off: low antral pH causes somatostatin release from D cells, inhibiting gastrin; duodenal acid releases secretin
questions.explanation: Acid secretion starts before food arrives, peaks as it is in the stomach, and is switched off by negative feedback as chyme moves on. The same chemical, acid, drives both the stimulation and the shutdown.

questions.stem: Compare gastrin, secretin and cholecystokinin by cell of origin, stimulus and main actions, and explain how secretin and CCK together neutralise and digest chyme in the duodenum.
markingGuide: Gastrin: G cells in the antrum; stimulated by peptides, distension and vagus; stimulates parietal acid secretion and mucosal growth
Secretin: S cells in the duodenum; stimulated by acid; stimulates bicarbonate from pancreatic and bile ducts; inhibits gastric acid
CCK: I cells in the duodenum and jejunum; stimulated by fatty acids and amino acids; stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion and gallbladder contraction, relaxes the sphincter of Oddi
Secretin (bicarbonate) raises duodenal pH so that pancreatic enzymes can act
CCK delivers enzymes and bile for protein and fat digestion
Both slow gastric emptying and reduce acid secretion
questions.explanation: The duodenum monitors its own contents through these hormones. Acid prompts neutralisation by bicarbonate and fat or protein prompts delivery of enzymes and bile.
